title: Judas and Pilate's wife (Matthew 27:1–26)
hookLine: silver handed back, a warning from a dream, and a bowl of water before the crowd
carry: have nothing to do with him
tomorrow: darkness over the land, a torn curtain, and a soldier says what?

lines: I HAVE BETRAYED THE INNOCENT BLOOD.
cards: Cool water running over your hands at a sink: an ordinary feeling from any day. This chapter has a washing that isn't ordinary. But first, morning.
Judas sees that Jesus is condemned and brings the thirty pieces of silver back to the chief priests and elders: "I have sinned in that I have betrayed the innocent blood."
The answer is short and cold: "What is that to us? see thou to that." Hold onto that phrase. It comes back, with water.

teach.b: Judas throws the silver down in the Temple and goes and hangs himself. Matthew tells it in one sentence, and this lesson will too.
If that lands heavy today, in the US you can call or text 988, or reach local emergency help wherever you are. Now Pontius Pilate, the Roman governor. He asks Jesus, "Art thou the King of the Jews?"
Jesus says, "Thou sayest," and then nothing more, "insomuch that the governor marvelled greatly." Pilate offers the crowd a choice, Barabbas or Jesus.
And while he sits on the judgment seat, a message comes from his wife: "Have thou nothing to do with that just man: for I have suffered many things this day in a dream because of him."
Matthew never names her, and she never appears again.
The crowd calls for crucifixion. Then the water.
Pilate takes it and washes his hands before the multitude: "I am innocent of the blood of this just person: see ye to it." Hear the echo. The priests to Judas: see thou to that.
Pilate to the crowd: see ye to it.

teach.h: HAVE NOTHING TO DO WITH HIM.
teach.b: Each hands the weight to someone else. Washing hands to declare innocence was an old sign; Israel's law has elders do it. But Pilate still releases Barabbas and delivers Jesus to be crucified.
The water is cool, and his hands are not clean of it.

how: Christians who say the Apostles' Creed or the Nicene Creed name Pilate in it (suffered under Pontius Pilate), and some churches read Matthew 27 aloud on Palm Sunday or Good Friday.

games.q: what does “judas and pilate's wife” mean?
o: two who saw the wrong: a betrayer and a warning wife
two disciples who fled when Jesus was arrested
the governor's servants who guarded the tomb

games.q: judas and Pilate's wife — tap the pairs.
p: I have betrayed the innocent blood
washes his hands: see ye to it

s: in Matthew, washing his hands makes Pilate innocent
he still releases Barabbas and delivers Jesus to be crucified. the water doesn't change what he does next.
Pilate's wife warned him because of a dream
"I have suffered many things this day in a dream because of him."
Matthew tells us the name of Pilate's wife
he never names her. later tradition gave her one.

games.q: you're about to sign a lease. your sister texts: 'i have a really bad feeling about that landlord. read the reviews first.' what does Pilate's story suggest?
o: stop and take the warning seriously before you decide.
ignore it: a bad feeling isn't evidence.
sign first, and read the reviews after.
games.why: the warning reached Pilate on the judgment seat, before the choice: have thou nothing to do with that just man. he heard it, and went ahead anyway.

practice: If there's a sink nearby, run cool water over your hands and feel it; if not, press your palms together. Name one person you're tempted to call not my problem.
Then, instead of washing them off, hold your hands cupped and open, as if they were still in them. Breathe there for a while, hands open, keeping them.

wordCard.voice: Judas and Pilate's wife. A man who tried to give the silver back, and a woman who sent a warning her husband washed away.

orig.note: Greek: dream; Pilate's wife suffered many things in a dream (Matthew 27:19).

carryVoice: Your line: have nothing to do with him, her warning, and the water couldn't wash it out. Go gently.
